Jaworzno Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Jaworzno, Poland

Not demolished. Jaworzno, founded before 1229 (town rights only in 1901), recorded its first Jewish settlers in the early 18th century; population grew from 15 in 1748 to 1,325 (10%) by 1910. Before this cemetery's founding, likely in the second half of the 19th century on private land owned by Jakób Bester (later transferred to the 'Chesed v'Emes' charity association), local Jews were buried in Będzin, Chrzanów, or Trzebinia. In spring 1940, Jews from Katowice, Chorzów, and Siemianowice were relocated to Jaworzno; on July 12-13, 1942, all 2,092 local Jews were deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau, with the last two families following on August 1, 1943. The last cemetery burial occurred in 1942. Today's grounds cover only about a quarter of the original site, the rest lost to a road (Aleja Józefa Piłsudskiego) built through it. A 2012 book, published with Municipal Museum support, documented the cemetery's full tombstone inventory.
